intro: Pick up any Qur'an, in any country, and it has the same shape. It has 114 chapters, called surahs. It has about 6,200 verses, called ayahs. It is split into 30 parts so it can be read in a month. In this unit you will learn that map. You will find out why the long surahs come first, what the labels Meccan and Medinan mean, and where three famous passages sit.

But the Qur'an is not only a book on a shelf. Muslims believe it was spoken before it was written. So this unit also follows the sound. You will meet the rules for reciting it, the people who know it all by heart, and the nights of Ramadan when it is heard from start to finish. You will see how the words became beautiful writing on walls and pages.

By the end, you will be able to find any verse from its two numbers, explain what a juz' and a hafiz are, and describe why Muslims keep the Arabic even when they read a translation. You will describe all of this the way a careful student does: "Muslims believe," "the Qur'an says," and "historians note."
bigQuestion: How is the Qur'an put together, and how do Muslims keep it alive in voice, memory and art?

title: The Shape of the Qur'an

chapters.title: 114 Surahs, 30 Parts
chapters.bigQuestion: How is the Qur'an put together, and how do Muslims find their way around it?

story.title: Thirty Bookmarks
story.kicker: On the first night of Ramadan, a family sets thirty paper strips inside one book.
paragraphs: It is the first night of Ramadan in Chicago. Samir's mother spreads thirty strips of green paper on the kitchen table. Each strip has a number, from 1 to 30. Samir asks what they are for. "Bookmarks," she says. "One for each night of the month."

She takes the family's Qur'an down from its shelf. It is a thick book with a soft cover. She opens it and slides the first bookmark in near the front. Then she turns a good many pages and slides in the second. She keeps going until all thirty are in place.

Samir counts the pages between two bookmarks. About twenty. "So each night we read one part?" he asks. His mother nods. "Muslims call each part a juz'. There are thirty. If you read one part each night, you finish the whole book by the end of Ramadan."

That night the family reads the first part together. It starts with a short surah of seven lines. Then it moves into a very long one. Samir notices something. The long surah goes on and on. But the last pages of the book, which he peeks at, are full of tiny surahs, some only three lines long.
"Why are the long ones at the front and the short ones at the back?" he asks. His mother smiles. "Good question. That is one of the first things to learn about this book."
story.think: Why might a family want thirty bookmarks in one book? What could dividing a book into equal parts help a reader do?

lessons.title: Surahs and Ayahs
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an has 114 surahs (chapters) made of about 6,200 ayahs (verses).
reading: The Qur'an is the holy book of Muslims. It is divided into 114 chapters. Each chapter is called a *surah*. Some surahs are very long. Surah 2 has 286 verses. Some are very short. Surah 108 has only three. Every surah has a name, such as The Cow, The Bee or The Opening.

Each surah is made of verses. A verse is called an *ayah*. The word ayah also means "a sign." Muslims believe each verse is a sign from God. Altogether the Qur'an has about 6,200 ayahs. Different counting systems give slightly different totals, so people say "about."

When Muslims point to a verse, they give two numbers. The first is the surah. The second is the ayah. So 2:255 means surah 2, verse 255. It is a little like a street address. Once you know the two numbers, you can find any verse in any copy of the book.

words.d: a chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114 of them
a verse of the Qur'an; the word also means "a sign"

lessons.title: Thirty Parts for Thirty Nights
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an is also split into 30 equal parts, called juz', so it can be read in one month.
reading: The 114 surahs are not all the same size. So Muslims also divide the book another way. They cut it into 30 parts of about equal length. Each part is called a *juz'*. The plural is ajza'. The juz' does not follow surah lines. One juz' can end in the middle of a surah.

Why 30? Because many Muslims want to read the whole Qur'an during *Ramadan*. Ramadan is the month of fasting. It lasts 29 or 30 days. One juz' a night means the whole book in one month. In many mosques, the reciter reads one juz' each night in special evening prayers.

Printed Qur'ans mark each juz' in the margin. Some also mark smaller pieces. Each juz' has two halves, called hizb. Each hizb has four quarters. Readers use these marks to keep their place. A child learning to read might aim for one quarter a day.

words.d: one of the 30 roughly equal parts of the Qur'an
the Muslim month of fasting, when many Muslims read the whole Qur'an

lessons.title: Why the Long Ones Come First
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an is arranged roughly from longest surah to shortest, not in the order Muslims believe the verses came.
reading: Open a Qur'an and look at the size of the surahs. After the short first surah, the second is the longest in the book. Then the surahs slowly get shorter. Near the end they are tiny. This is the pattern: roughly longest to shortest. It is not a perfect rule, but it is close.

This is not the order the words came, according to Muslim belief. Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad over about 23 years. Tradition says the first verses to come were the start of surah 96. Yet surah 96 sits near the back. So the book's order and the time order are different.

Muslim scholars have written about why the surahs sit where they do. Most Muslims believe the Prophet himself showed where each part belonged. Some scholars think the order shows patterns of meaning. Historians describe the order as it is. Either way, readers learn to use the book as it is arranged.

words.d: made known; Muslims believe God revealed the Qur'an to Muhammad
what a community has passed down and taught for a long time

look.title: Two Orders
look.text: Book order: surah 1 (7 verses), surah 2 (286 verses), surah 3 (200 verses) ... surah 112 (4 verses), surah 114 (6 verses). Time order, as Muslim tradition tells it: the first words revealed were the first verses of surah 96, which sits near the back of the book.

check.q: How are the surahs mostly arranged?
choices: In the order they were revealed
check.why: After surah 1, the surahs run roughly from the longest to the shortest.

check.q: According to Muslim tradition, which surah has the first verses revealed?
check.why: Tradition says the first words revealed were the opening verses of surah 96, near the back of the book.

check.q: Over about how many years do Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed?
check.why: Muslims believe the revelation came piece by piece over about 23 years.

lessons.title: Mecca and Medina
lessons.mainIdea: Each surah is labeled Meccan or Medinan, after the city where Muslims believe it was revealed.
reading: Muslim tradition tells of two cities in Muhammad's life. He was born in *Mecca*. He lived there until he was about 52. Then he and his followers moved to *Medina*, a city to the north. That move happened in the year 622. Muslims count their calendar from it.

Every surah carries a label. It says Meccan or Medinan. The label tells where Muslims believe the surah was revealed. About 86 surahs are called Meccan. About 28 are called Medinan. Printed Qur'ans put the label at the top of each surah.

Scholars notice that the two groups sound different. Meccan surahs are often short. They speak about one God and about the Day of Judgment. Medinan surahs are often longer. They speak about how a community should live together. Knowing the label helps a reader understand what a surah is doing.

words.d: the city in Arabia where Muhammad was born; Muslims pray facing it
the city Muhammad moved to in 622; Muslims believe many later surahs came there

look.title: Meccan and Medinan Surahs

check.q: Which group of surahs is often longer and speaks about community life?

lessons.title: The Opening
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Fatiha, the first surah, is a seven-line prayer that Muslims recite in every daily prayer.
reading: The first surah of the Qur'an is called *Al-Fatiha*. The name means "The Opening." It has only seven ayahs. Yet Muslims say it more than any other part of the book. They recite it in every unit of their daily prayers. A Muslim may say it more than fifteen times a day.

The surah is a prayer spoken to God. It begins with praise. It calls God the Lord of all worlds, full of mercy. It says that God is the master of the Day of Judgment. Then the speaker says, in simple words: You alone we worship, and from You alone we ask help.

The last lines are a request. The speaker asks God to show the straight path. It is the path of those God has blessed. It is not the path of those who earned anger or who went astray. Muslim scholars call Al-Fatiha a summary of the whole book. Some call it "the mother of the book."

words.d: "The Opening," surah 1 of the Qur'an, a prayer of seven verses
to say aloud from memory, often with a rhythm

look.title: Al-Fatiha in Simple Words
look.text: Praise belongs to God, Lord of all the worlds, the Kind, the Merciful, who rules the Day of Judgment. You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help. Show us the straight path, the path of those You have blessed, not of those who earned anger, and not of those who went astray.
look.cite: Qur'an 1:1-7, Al-Fatiha (The Opening), paraphrased in simple words from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: Who is speaking, and to whom? What does the speaker ask for?

check.q: What does the name Al-Fatiha mean?
check.why: Al-Fatiha means "The Opening." It is the first surah.

check.q: How many ayahs are in Al-Fatiha?
check.why: Al-Fatiha has seven short verses.

check.q: What do the last lines of Al-Fatiha ask for?

check.why: The surah ends by asking God to show the straight path.

lessons.title: The Throne Verse
lessons.mainIdea: The Throne Verse (2:255) describes God as the one living, all-knowing ruler, and many Muslims memorize it early.
reading: Deep inside the long second surah is one famous ayah. It is verse 255. Muslims call it Ayat al-Kursi, the *Throne Verse*. Many Muslim children learn it early. Many adults say it after each prayer and before sleep. You may see it on wall hangings in Muslim homes.

The verse describes God. It says there is no god but God, the Living One, who never sleeps. It says God knows what is in front of people and behind them. It says God's throne, or kursi, reaches over the heavens and the earth. Keeping them is no burden for God.

Muslim scholars read the verse as a picture of *tawhid*. Tawhid means that God is one. Some readers take the throne as a real throne. Others read it as a way of saying God's power and knowledge cover everything. Both readings appear in Muslim commentaries.

words.d: Qur'an 2:255, a verse about God's power that many Muslims memorize
the Muslim belief that God is one

look.title: The Throne Verse in Simple Words
look.text: God: there is no god but God, the Living, the One who keeps all things. Sleep does not take hold of God, and neither does tiredness. All that is in the heavens and the earth belongs to God. God knows what is before people and what is behind them. God's throne reaches over the heavens and the earth, and keeping them is no burden. God is the High, the Great.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:255, Al-Baqarah (The Cow), paraphrased in simple words from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: Pick two things the verse says about God. How might a Muslim reader feel saying this before sleep?

check.q: Where is the Throne Verse found?
check.why: The Throne Verse is 2:255, inside the long surah called The Cow.

check.q: What does tawhid mean?

check.why: Tawhid is the Muslim belief in one God. Scholars read the Throne Verse as a picture of it.

check.q: How do Muslim readers differ about the throne in the verse?

check.why: Muslim commentaries include both a literal reading and a reading of the throne as God's power and knowledge.

lessons.title: Four Lines on One God
lessons.mainIdea: Surah 112, Al-Ikhlas, states in four short lines the Muslim belief that God is one and has no equal.
reading: Near the end of the book is a tiny surah. It is number 112. Its name is *Al-Ikhlas*, which means sincerity, or pure faith. It has just four ayahs. Children often learn it right after Al-Fatiha. Many Muslims say it in their daily prayers.

The surah begins with the word "Say." Muslims believe God is telling Muhammad what to say. The message is short. God is one. God is the one everyone needs and who needs no one. God did not have children and was not born. Nothing is like God.

Muslim tradition says the Prophet called this surah worth a third of the Qur'an. Scholars explain why. They say the Qur'an has three big themes: God, the Day of Judgment, and how to live. This surah covers the first theme all by itself. That is why it matters so much to Muslims.

words.d: surah 112, four verses about God being one; the name means sincerity
a big idea that a book keeps coming back to

look.title: Surah 112 in Pickthall's Words
look.text: Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him.
look.cite: Qur'an 112:1-4, Al-Ikhlas, Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: Pickthall used old English words. Put each of the four lines into your own words. What is the one idea all four lines share?

check.q: How many ayahs does Al-Ikhlas have?
check.why: Al-Ikhlas is one of the shortest surahs, with four verses.

check.q: What is the main message of Al-Ikhlas?
choices: God is one and has no equal
check.why: All four lines say, in different ways, that God is one and nothing is like God.

check.q: According to Muslim tradition, what did the Prophet say about surah 112?
choices: It is worth a third of the Qur'an

check.why: Tradition reports him saying it equals a third of the Qur'an because it covers the theme of God.

lessons.title: In the Name of God
lessons.mainIdea: Every surah but one begins with the Bismillah, a line that names God as gracious and merciful.
reading: Look at the start of any surah. You will see the same line. In Arabic it begins "Bismillah." The whole line means: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Muslims call the line the *Bismillah*. It sits at the head of 113 surahs.

One surah does not begin with it. That is surah 9. Muslim scholars have long discussed why. Some say surah 9 continues surah 8. Others say its stern tone did not fit a line about mercy. No one is sure. But everyone agrees the line is missing there.

The line also appears inside surah 27. There it opens a letter that the king Sulayman (Solomon) sends to a queen. So the Bismillah is counted 114 times in the book. Muslims also say the line before eating or starting a task. It is one of the most spoken lines in the world.

words.d: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"; the line at the head of 113 surahs
kind and forgiving, even when someone has done wrong

look.title: The Missing Line
look.text: Surah 8 ends. On the next page, surah 9 begins, but the usual first line is not there. A student asks the teacher why. The teacher says: "Some Muslim scholars think surahs 8 and 9 were once read as one long surah. Others think this surah's stern message did not fit a line about mercy. Nobody knows for certain."
look.prompt: The teacher gives two reasons and then says nobody is certain. Why is it honest to say that? How is that different from making up an answer?

check.q: What does the Bismillah say?
choices: Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds
In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful
Say: He is God, the One
check.why: The Bismillah is the line "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful."

check.q: Which surah does not begin with the Bismillah?
check.why: Surah 9 is the only surah without the Bismillah at its head.

check.q: Where does the Bismillah appear inside a surah?
choices: In a letter from Sulayman in surah 27
check.why: In surah 27, the line opens a letter from Sulayman (Solomon) to a queen.

lessons.title: A Book Meant to Be Heard
lessons.mainIdea: The name Qur'an means "the recitation," because the book was heard aloud before it was written.
reading: The book's own name tells you something. *Qur'an* is an Arabic word. It comes from a word that means to read aloud or recite. So the name means "the recitation." The name points to a voice. Muslims believe the words were spoken to Muhammad, who spoke them to others.

The very first word revealed, according to Muslim tradition, was a command. It was "Iqra!" The word means "Read!" or "Recite!" It opens surah 96. Muhammad could not read or write, as tradition tells it. His followers learned the words by heart and said them back.

Even today, most Muslims meet the Qur'an first by ear. A parent sings it to a baby. A teacher says a line and the class repeats. In the next chapter you will see how the spoken book became a written one, and how Muslims keep the sound alive.

words.d: the holy book of Muslims; the name means "the recitation"
Arabic for "Read!" or "Recite!"; the first word Muslims believe was revealed

check.why: Qur'an comes from an Arabic word for reciting or reading aloud.

check.q: What does the word Iqra mean?

lessons.title: Finding Your Way
lessons.mainIdea: With surah numbers, ayah numbers and juz' marks, a reader can find any spot in the Qur'an quickly.
reading: Now you know the Qur'an's map. It has 114 surahs. Each has a name, a number and a label, Meccan or Medinan. Each surah is made of numbered ayahs. Each begins with the Bismillah, except surah 9. And the whole book is split into 30 juz' for reading over a month.

To find a passage, start with the surah number. The table of contents lists all 114. Then count ayahs. Printed copies put a small number at the end of each ayah. It usually sits inside a little circle or flower shape. Find the number, and you have the verse.

Try it with three famous spots. Al-Fatiha is 1:1-7, at the very front. The Throne Verse is 2:255, deep in the second surah. Al-Ikhlas is 112:1-4, near the back. Muslims around the world use the same numbers. A child in Chicago and a grandmother in Cairo can turn to the same line.

words.d: a list of a book's chapters and where each one starts
a short section of a text, such as one or a few verses

look.title: Three Readers, One Verse
look.text: A teacher writes 2:255 on the board. A girl in Chicago opens a printed Qur'an and turns to surah 2. A boy in Cairo opens an app and types the numbers. A grandfather in Indonesia recites the verse from memory without opening anything. All three arrive at the same words.
look.prompt: What did each reader need to know to find the verse? What does this show about how the numbers help Muslims around the world?

check.q: Which surah has no Bismillah at its head?

review.why: Thirty juz' match the nights of Ramadan, so the whole book can be finished in the month.

review.q: Which statement about the order of the surahs is correct?
choices: They are in the order they were revealed
After surah 1, they run roughly longest to shortest
review.why: The book's order is roughly by length, not by the time Muslims believe the verses came.

review.q: What does the label "Meccan" mean on a surah?
choices: Muslims believe it was revealed in Mecca
It is about the city of Mecca
It must be read in Mecca
It was written by people from Mecca
review.why: Meccan and Medinan labels tell where Muslims believe the surah was revealed.

review.q: Which passage do Muslims recite in every unit of daily prayer?
review.why: Al-Fatiha, The Opening, is recited in every unit of the daily prayers.

review.q: Which surah is four lines long and is about God being one?
review.why: Al-Ikhlas, surah 112, has four verses on God's oneness.

review.q: What does the name Qur'an mean?
review.why: Qur'an means "the recitation," a book meant to be heard aloud.

chapters.title: Reciting, Memorizing and Writing It Beautifully
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do Muslims keep the Qur'an alive as sound, memory and art, not just as words on a page?

story.title: Nadia Knows It by Heart
story.kicker: A fourth grader in Chicago stands up with no book in her hands, and the room goes quiet.
paragraphs: It is share day in Ms. Ortiz's fourth-grade class on the North Side of Chicago. Some students bring a photo or a favorite book. Nadia brings nothing. She walks to the front with her hands empty. "I'm going to say a surah from the Qur'an," she tells the class. "It's called Maryam. I learned the whole thing."

She closes her eyes and begins. The words are Arabic, so most of the class cannot understand them. But they can hear something. Nadia's voice rises and falls. Some sounds stretch out long. Some stop short. The lines end with the same sound, over and over, like a soft rhyme.

Nadia recites for almost ten minutes. Nobody moves. When she stops, a boy in the back asks, "How many words was that?" Nadia thinks. "I don't know. But it's 98 verses." Another student asks how she learned it. "A little every day," she says. "My teacher at the mosque says one line. I say it back. Then two lines. It took me all year."

Ms. Ortiz asks what the surah is about. Nadia says it tells about Maryam, the mother of Isa. "That's Mary and Jesus," she adds. "It's a surah named after a woman." A girl in the front says her church has a story about Mary too. Nadia nods. "Some of it is the same, and some is different."
On the way to lunch, the boy from the back catches up to Nadia. "Ten minutes with no paper," he says. "How do you not forget?" Nadia shrugs. "You say it every day. Then it stays."
story.think: Nadia learned 98 verses by saying them a little at a time. Why might a person choose to learn a whole book by heart instead of just reading it?

lessons.title: Spoken First
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe the Qur'an was spoken and heard for years before it was gathered into a written book.
reading: The Qur'an did not start as a book on a shelf. Muslim tradition says the words came to Muhammad a few at a time, over about 23 years. He spoke them to his followers. They said them back and learned them by heart. Some wrote pieces on leather, bone or palm leaves. But mostly the words lived in voices.

The Qur'an itself talks about being *recited*. To recite means to say aloud from memory. One verse tells the Prophet to recite the Qur'an slowly and clearly (73:4). Another says that God sent it down in the month of Ramadan (2:185). Muslims read these verses as a sign that the book is meant for the ear.

After the Prophet died in 632, his followers worried. Many who knew the words by heart had died in battles. According to Muslim tradition, the leader Abu Bakr ordered the pieces gathered. Later, the leader Uthman had a standard copy made, around the year 650. That is how, as Muslims tell it, the voice became a book.

words.d: said aloud from memory, often with a careful rhythm
one agreed copy that all other copies are made to match

look.title: Recite It Slowly
look.text: The verse tells the Prophet to stay up part of the night and to recite the Qur'an in a slow, clear and measured way.
look.cite: Qur'an 73:4, Al-Muzzammil (The Enshrouded One), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: Why might slow, clear reciting matter for a text that people learn by ear?

check.q: According to Muslim tradition, how did the Qur'an first spread?
choices: By people learning it by heart and saying it aloud
check.why: Tradition says the words were spoken, heard and memorized before they were gathered as a book.

check.q: Which leader, as Muslims tell it, had a standard copy of the Qur'an made around 650?
check.why: Muslim tradition says Uthman had a standard copy made around the year 650. Abu Bakr had the pieces gathered earlier.

check.q: What does 73:4 tell the Prophet to do?
choices: Write the Qur'an in a book
Recite the Qur'an slowly and clearly
check.why: The verse tells him to recite in a slow, measured way.

lessons.title: Saying It Right
lessons.mainIdea: Tajwid is the set of rules for reciting the Qur'an correctly, sound by sound.
reading: Listen to a Muslim recite the Qur'an. You will hear long, stretched sounds. You will hear soft hums through the nose. You will hear clear stops. None of this is random. It follows rules. The rules are called *tajwid*. The word means making something good or beautiful.

Tajwid tells the reciter where each sound comes from in the mouth and throat. It says which vowels to stretch and for how long. It says where a reader may pause and where a pause would change the meaning. Muslims believe the rules keep the words the way the Prophet said them.

Children learn tajwid slowly. First they learn the Arabic letters. Then they learn to join them. A teacher says a line, and the student copies the sound. Mistakes are fixed gently. A student who reads with good tajwid is praised. Muslims in Chicago learn it at mosques and at weekend schools, just as students do in Cairo or Jakarta.

words.d: the rules for saying each sound of the Qur'an correctly when reciting
an open speech sound, like a, i or u; in Arabic some vowels are held long

look.title: Where to Pause
look.text: A reciter reads the line "Those who believe and do good works" but runs out of breath after "Those who believe." A tajwid teacher stops her. "If you must breathe there, go back and read the whole line again. Stopping in the middle changes what the listener hears."
look.prompt: Why would a pause in the wrong place change the meaning? Give an example of an English sentence where a pause matters.

check.q: What is tajwid?
choices: A written copy of the Qur'an
The rules for reciting the Qur'an correctly
check.why: Tajwid is the set of rules for pronouncing and pacing each sound when reciting.

check.q: What does the word tajwid mean?
check.why: Tajwid comes from an Arabic root meaning to make good or beautiful.

check.q: Why do Muslims believe tajwid matters?
choices: It keeps the words the way the Prophet said them
It lets readers skip hard verses
It is needed to read English
check.why: Muslims believe the rules protect the sound of the words as they were first recited.

lessons.title: A Whole Book by Heart
lessons.mainIdea: A person who has memorized the entire Qur'an is called a hafiz, and there are millions of them around the world.
reading: Some people know the whole Qur'an by heart. All 114 surahs. All 6,200 ayahs. Such a person is called a *hafiz*. A girl or woman is called a hafiza. The word means "guardian" or "keeper." Muslims believe a hafiz helps keep the book safe by carrying it in memory.

Muslim tradition says several of the Prophet's companions knew the whole Qur'an by heart. Since then, every generation has had memorizers. Today they number in the millions, though no exact count exists. Some are children as young as eight or nine. Some are grandparents. They live in every country where Muslims live.

How do they do it? Slowly, and every day. A student learns a few lines, then repeats them. The next day, a few more. Old lines are reviewed so they do not fade. It often takes two to five years. Many Muslim families hold a party when a child finishes. Some countries and cities hold contests for the best young reciters.

words.d: a person who has memorized the whole Qur'an; a woman or girl is a hafiza
all the people born and living around the same time

look.title: Learn It and Teach It
look.text: A well-known saying reported from the Prophet says that the best people are those who learn the Qur'an and then teach it to others.
look.cite: Hadith reported in Sahih al-Bukhari (9th century), paraphrased
look.prompt: Why might teaching the Qur'an count as much as learning it, in this saying?

check.q: What is a hafiz?
choices: A person who leads a mosque
A person who has memorized the whole Qur'an
check.why: A hafiz has the whole Qur'an by heart. The word means keeper or guardian.

check.q: About how long does it often take to memorize the whole Qur'an?
check.why: Most memorizers work a little every day for two to five years.

check.q: Why do Muslims value a hafiz?
choices: A hafiz helps keep the book safe in memory
A hafiz can write in gold
A hafiz gets to skip Ramadan
A hafiz owns the only copy
check.why: Muslims believe memorizers help guard the Qur'an by carrying it in memory across generations.

lessons.title: Ramadan Nights
lessons.mainIdea: During Ramadan, many Muslims hear the whole Qur'an recited in the mosque, one part each night.
reading: *Ramadan* is the ninth month of the Muslim calendar. Muslims fast from dawn to sunset. They do not eat or drink during the day. The Qur'an says God sent the book down in this month (2:185). So Muslims treat Ramadan as the Qur'an's own month.

After the sunset meal, many Muslims go to the mosque for extra night prayers. They are called tarawih. In many mosques, the reciter reads one juz' each night. Over 29 or 30 nights, the people hear the whole Qur'an. People stand quietly and listen. Some follow along in a copy of their own.

Muslims also honor one special night near the end of the month. It is called Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power. Surah 97 says the Qur'an was sent down on that night. It calls the night better than a thousand months. Many Muslims stay up late that night to pray and recite.

words.d: the ninth month of the Muslim calendar, a month of fasting and Qur'an reading
Laylat al-Qadr, a night in Ramadan when Muslims believe the Qur'an was sent down

look.title: The Night of Power
look.text: Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Power. Ah, what will convey unto thee what the Night of Power is! The Night of Power is better than a thousand months.
look.cite: Qur'an 97:1-3, Al-Qadr (Power), Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: Who is "We" in this passage, as Muslims read it? What does the surah say about the night?

check.q: What do Muslims do during the days of Ramadan?
check.why: Ramadan is the month of fasting. Muslims do not eat or drink from dawn until sunset.

check.q: What happens at tarawih prayers in many mosques?
choices: The Qur'an is written out by hand
One juz' of the Qur'an is recited each night
The whole Qur'an is read in one night
check.why: Many mosques recite one juz' per night so the whole Qur'an is heard over the month.

check.q: What does surah 97 say about the Night of Power?
choices: It is the first night of the year
It is a night of feasting
It is the night of the hijra
It is better than a thousand months
check.why: Surah 97 says the Night of Power is better than a thousand months.

lessons.title: The Written Copy
lessons.mainIdea: A written copy of the Qur'an is called a mushaf, and Muslims handle it with special care.
reading: Muslims use a special word for a written copy of the Qur'an. It is *mushaf*. The word means a set of pages bound together. The Qur'an is the words. A mushaf is one copy of the words on paper. There are millions of mushafs in the world, but Muslims believe there is only one Qur'an.

Muslims treat a mushaf with care. Many wash their hands before touching it. Families keep it on a high shelf, often wrapped in cloth. It is never placed on the floor. It is not stacked under other books. When a copy wears out, many Muslims bury it or store it rather than throw it away.

The oldest mushaf pages are very old. Two pages kept at a library in Birmingham, England, were tested by scientists. The test dated the animal skin to the 600s, the century of the Prophet. Historians note that the words on them match the Qur'an read today. Muslims see this as a sign of careful copying.

words.d: a written or printed copy of the Qur'an
a book or page written by hand, before printing

look.title: One Book, Many Copies
look.text: Picture a shelf in a Chicago mosque. On it sit twenty green mushafs. Some are big with large letters for older eyes. Some are small enough for a pocket. One is very old and its cover is worn. A teacher says: "Twenty copies, one Qur'an."
look.prompt: What does the teacher mean by "twenty copies, one Qur'an"? How is this like or unlike twenty copies of a school library book?

check.q: What is a mushaf?
choices: A written copy of the Qur'an
check.why: A mushaf is one physical copy of the Qur'an on pages.

check.q: Which shows the care Muslims give a mushaf?
choices: Keeping it on a high shelf and never under other books
check.why: Muslims keep the mushaf high and clean, and never on the floor or under other books.

check.q: What did scientists find about the Birmingham pages?
check.why: Testing dated the animal skin of the pages to the 600s, the Prophet's own century.

lessons.title: Dots and Marks
lessons.mainIdea: Early Arabic writing had few dots or vowel marks; later scribes added them so every reader could say the words the same way.
reading: Arabic is written from right to left. It has 28 letters. Many letters share the same basic shape. Small dots above or below tell them apart. In the earliest Qur'an pages, those dots were often left out. Short vowels were not written at all. Readers who already knew the words by heart did not need them.

As Islam spread, many new Muslims did not speak Arabic as a first language. Reading without dots was hard for them. So, over the next two or three hundred years, *scribes* added the dots. They added small marks for short vowels. They added signs for where to stretch a sound or stop. The page began to show what the voice already knew.

Today a printed mushaf carries all of these marks. It also has ayah numbers, juz' marks and notes on where to pause. In 1924, scholars in Cairo, Egypt, printed a carefully checked edition. Most printed Qur'ans today follow it. Muslims see the marks as helpers. The sound, they say, came first.

words.d: people whose job was to copy books by hand
one printed version of a book

look.title: From Voice to Printed Page
rows: Standard copy under Uthman (as tradition tells it)
Dots and vowel marks in common use, by about
look.cite: Dates as commonly given by historians of the Qur'an's text; early dates are approximate
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the first standard copy and the printed Cairo edition? What changed on the page in that time?

check.q: Which way is Arabic written?
check.why: Arabic runs from right to left across the page.

check.q: Why did scribes add dots and vowel marks to the Qur'an?
choices: So readers who did not know the words by heart could read them correctly
check.why: As Islam spread to non-Arabic speakers, the marks helped every reader say the words the same way.

check.q: What happened in Cairo in 1924?
choices: A carefully checked printed edition of the Qur'an was made
The Qur'an was translated into English
check.why: The 1924 Cairo edition is the printed text most Qur'ans follow today.

lessons.title: Writing as Art
lessons.mainIdea: Calligraphy, beautiful handwriting, is the main art of the Qur'an, and its styles have names and long histories.
reading: Open an old mushaf in a museum. The letters are not just clear. They are beautiful. Some are thick and gold. Some curve like waves. This art is called *calligraphy*. The word means beautiful writing. For Muslims, writing the Qur'an well is a way of honoring it.

Calligraphy has styles, the way music has styles. The earliest Qur'ans used a style called Kufic. Its letters are straight and boxy. Later a rounder style called Naskh became common. It is easier to read. Most printed Qur'ans today use a form of Naskh. Other styles bend and stack letters into shapes.

Great calligraphers were famous, like great painters are today. One was Ibn Muqla, who lived in Baghdad and died in 940. Tradition says he worked out rules for the size and shape of each letter. Calligraphers still train for years. They copy a master's lines until their hand learns the form.

words.d: the art of beautiful handwriting
an early, straight-lined style of Arabic writing used in old Qur'ans
a rounded, easy-to-read style of Arabic writing used in most printed Qur'ans

look.title: Two Styles, Same Words
look.text: Imagine two pages side by side. On the left, thick, square, gold letters march in straight lines with wide gaps. That is Kufic, from an early mushaf. On the right, smaller letters flow and curve, with dots and small marks above and below. That is Naskh, from a printed mushaf today. Both pages hold the same verse.
look.prompt: Which page would be easier for a new reader? Which might be made to be admired? What does each choice say about who the page was for?

check.q: What is calligraphy?
check.why: Calligraphy means beautiful writing. It is the main art of the Qur'an.

check.q: Which style has straight, boxy letters and was used in early Qur'ans?
check.why: Kufic is the early, angular style. Naskh is the rounder, later style.

check.q: Who was Ibn Muqla?
choices: A famous calligrapher in Baghdad who died in 940
The leader who made the standard copy
The scholar who printed the Cairo edition
check.why: Ibn Muqla was a master calligrapher; tradition says he set rules for letter shapes.

lessons.title: Words Instead of Pictures
lessons.mainIdea: Most Muslims do not make pictures of God or the prophets, so the words of the Qur'an became the art of mosques and books.
reading: Walk into a mosque and look around. You will not see a painting of God. You will not see a statue of Muhammad. Most Muslims believe such pictures should not be made. They worry a picture might be worshipped, or might make God seem small. So, in most Muslim art, God and the prophets are not shown.

Instead, the walls carry words. Verses of the Qur'an are carved in stone. They are painted on tiles. They run in bands around domes and doorways. A famous early example is the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, finished around 691. Long lines of Qur'an verses circle its inside walls.

Beside the words, artists use *geometric* patterns. Stars, hexagons and knots repeat across a wall. Vines and flowers curl around the letters. Muslims say the patterns point to order and to the oneness of God. Not every Muslim culture has followed the same rules. Some Persian and Turkish books did show the Prophet, often with his face veiled. But in mosques and in mushafs, the words are the art.

words.d: made of shapes like squares, stars and circles that repeat in a pattern
a rounded roof, common on mosques

look.title: Reading a Wall
look.text: Picture the inside of a mosque in Chicago. Above the doorway, a band of gold Arabic letters curves across blue tile. A visitor asks what it says. The guide answers: "It is the Throne Verse. Many mosques choose it. People read it as they walk in." Below the band, a pattern of eight-pointed stars repeats to the floor.
look.prompt: Why might a community choose a verse for its doorway instead of a picture? What might the repeating stars mean to the people who made them?

check.q: Why do most Muslims not make pictures of God or the prophets?
choices: Paint is not allowed in mosques
They worry a picture might be worshipped or make God seem small
check.why: Most Muslims believe pictures of God and the prophets should not be made, partly to avoid worshipping them.

check.q: What often takes the place of pictures in a mosque?
choices: Qur'an verses in calligraphy and geometric patterns
check.why: Mosque walls carry Qur'an verses in beautiful writing and repeating geometric patterns.

check.q: Which early building has long lines of Qur'an verses on its inside walls?
choices: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem
check.why: The Dome of the Rock, finished around 691, carries Qur'an verses around its inside walls.

lessons.title: The Qur'an in English
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an has been translated into many languages, and Muslims usually call a translation "the meaning," not the Qur'an itself.
reading: Most Muslims do not speak Arabic as their first language. There are about 1.9 billion Muslims, and estimates vary. They live in Indonesia, Pakistan, Nigeria, Turkey, the United States and many other places. So people have *translated* the Qur'an into hundreds of languages, including English.

The first full English translation from Arabic was made by George Sale in 1734. Others followed. In 1930, an English Muslim named Marmaduke Pickthall made the translation this course uses. He called it The Meaning of the Glorious Koran. He did not call it the Qur'an. He said only the Arabic is the Qur'an. A translation gives the meaning.

Most Muslims agree with Pickthall on this. A translation helps a reader understand. But it is a person's best try at the meaning. Two translators may choose different English words for one Arabic word. That is why many Muslim homes keep a copy with Arabic on one side and English on the other.

words.d: put into another language
a person who puts a text into another language

look.title: English Translations Through Time
look.cite: Publication dates of well-known English translations of the Qur'an
look.prompt: Which translation is the oldest? How many years passed between Sale and Pickthall?

check.q: What did Pickthall call his 1930 English translation?
choices: The Meaning of the Glorious Koran
check.why: Pickthall used "The Meaning" in his title because he held that only the Arabic is the Qur'an.

check.q: Who made the first full English translation from Arabic, in 1734?
check.why: George Sale's 1734 translation was the first complete English version made from the Arabic.

check.q: Why do many Muslim homes keep a copy with Arabic and English side by side?
choices: Because English is the holy language
To read the Arabic and understand it with the English
Because it is required by law
check.why: The Arabic is the Qur'an for Muslims; the English helps readers understand the meaning.

lessons.title: Why the Arabic Stays
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims everywhere recite the Qur'an in Arabic, because they believe the Arabic words themselves are the revelation.
reading: A Muslim boy in Chicago prays in Arabic. So does a girl in Senegal and a grandmother in Malaysia. None of them may speak Arabic at home. Yet all of them recite Al-Fatiha in the same Arabic words. Why not use their own languages?

Muslims believe the Arabic words are the *revelation* itself. The Qur'an says of itself that it is an Arabic Qur'an, sent so that people could understand (12:2). For Muslims, the sound and the words go together. Changing the language would make a different text. So prayer stays in Arabic, and the translation is for study.

This shared language links Muslims across the world. A reciter from Egypt can lead prayer in Chicago. A child who learns Al-Fatiha in Detroit can pray in Mecca. Muslims say this is one of the ways the Qur'an makes them one community. Learning Arabic letters and sounds is part of growing up Muslim, in any country.

words.d: a message that Muslims believe God made known to a prophet
a group of people who share a way of life or belief

look.title: An Arabic Qur'an
look.text: The verse says that the Qur'an was sent down as an Arabic recitation so that its hearers might understand it.
look.cite: Qur'an 12:2, Yusuf (Joseph), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: The verse gives a reason for Arabic. What is it? How do Muslims who do not speak Arabic handle this today?

check.q: In what language do Muslims around the world recite the Qur'an in prayer?
check.why: Muslims believe the Arabic words are the revelation itself, so prayer stays in Arabic.

check.q: What do Muslims use a translation for?
choices: Replacing the Arabic in the mushaf
check.why: Translations help with understanding; recitation and prayer use the Arabic.

check.q: What does 12:2 say about the Qur'an?
choices: It was sent in every language
It was sent as an Arabic recitation so hearers could understand
It must be read in English
check.why: The verse describes the Qur'an as Arabic, sent so that its hearers might understand.

review.why: Tradition says the words were recited and memorized for years before they were gathered into a book.

review.q: What are the rules for reciting the Qur'an correctly called?
review.why: Tajwid is the set of rules for saying each sound and pause correctly.

choices: A written copy of the Qur'an
A girl or woman who has memorized the whole Qur'an
review.why: A hafiz or hafiza is a person who knows the whole Qur'an by heart.

review.q: Why do many mosques recite one juz' each night in Ramadan?
choices: Because each juz' is one surah
So the whole Qur'an is heard over the month
review.why: Thirty juz' fit the 29 or 30 nights of Ramadan.

choices: A written or printed copy of the Qur'an
review.why: A mushaf is one copy of the Qur'an on pages; Muslims believe there is one Qur'an but many mushafs.
